quote.text: A flaw was found in all python-ecdsa versions before 0.13.3

reading.notes: The project's own 0.13.3 release notes, as excerpted in S2, do not name CVE-2019-14859: they describe the fix under the number CVE-2019-14853, covering both a denial of service (DoS) from decoding malformed signatures and signature malleability. The advisory record (S1) describes only the acceptance of malformed signatures. What the sources describe is a signature whose bytes break the DER rules being accepted; they do not show a signature for a different message, or one made without the key, being accepted. The flaw is in reading signatures in DER form: the 0.13.2 DER reader (S4) lacks the shortest-form checks, and several of the length checks, that 0.13.3 has (S3). The signature decoder (S5) is given for 0.13.3 only, so the sources do not show whether its refusal of extra bytes after the signature is new.
reading.weakness: When python-ecdsa before 0.13.3 reads a signature written in DER form (a strict byte layout), it does not check that the bytes really follow the DER rules, such as writing numbers and lengths in their shortest form with no unneeded zero bytes. A signature whose bytes break those rules can still be accepted, so the same signature can be rewritten as different bytes that also pass (the advisory calls this a malleable signature).

weakness_quote.text: it did not correctly verify whether signatures used DER encoding. Without this verification, a malformed signature could be accepted, making the signature malleable.

reading.notes: The advisory covers two separate problems, and the kind above records only the first. (1) Wrong error type: this library reports a rejected signature by raising BadSignatureError (it returns True when the signature passes), so an error on a bad signature is not the fault by itself. The fault is a different error type raised for a malformed signature, and the program stops only if the calling code does not catch it. As other error types to catch, the advisory names UnexpectedDER, IndexError and AssertionError, and says that list has not been verified to be complete. This is not limited to DER signatures: for the default fixed-length format, 0.13.2 checks the length with an assert (S8) and 0.13.3 turns that case into BadSignatureError (S7, S3). (2) Loose DER reading, which the advisory calls signature malleability: with ecdsa.util.sigdecode_der, signatures that are not properly formatted DER are accepted. For example, 0.13.3 refuses a number padded with unnecessary zero bytes (S5) and the 0.13.2 code shown has no such check (S6). The advisory says this affects only applications that later sign the signatures or verify signatures of signatures, such as Bitcoin; the sources do not say that a signature for different data or from a different key is accepted. The advisory says there are no plans to backport the fix to earlier releases, and the 0.13.3 release notes (S2) name this CVE as fixed in that release.
reading.weakness: When given a malformed signature, VerifyingKey.verify() and verify_digest() can raise errors other than the documented BadSignatureError, and a program that does not catch them may stop. With the DER decoder (sigdecode_der) they also accept signatures that do not properly follow the DER byte format.

weakness_quote.text: Code using `VerifyingKey.verify()` and `VerifyingKey.verify_digest()` may receive exceptions other than the documented `BadSignatureError` when signatures are malformed. If those other exceptions are not caught, they may lead to program termination and thus Denial of Service

design.question: Does {program} refuse an ECDSA P-256 signature when one of its two numbers (r or s) is zero or outside the allowed range?
design.why: Why it matters: a program that does not refuse such numbers may accept a signature that the key's owner never made, and the published note for these cases says such a signature can be forged without even knowing the message, so changed data could pass as properly signed.

design.question: Does {program} refuse a signature whose numbers are valid but whose bytes break the strict DER rules, such as a length written in a longer form than needed or a number with unneeded zero bytes in front?
design.why: Why it matters: if a signature that breaks the DER rules is still accepted, the same signature can be rewritten as different bytes that also pass, which can mislead a system that relies on each signature having only one valid byte form.

design.question: Does {program} refuse a signature whose two numbers are right but whose bytes break the strict DER format, such as a length written in a longer form than needed or a number padded with extra zero bytes?
design.why: Why it matters: if a checker accepts several byte forms of one signature, anyone can rewrite a valid signature into a different-looking one that still passes, which the advisory says affects only applications that later sign the signatures or check signatures of signatures, such as Bitcoin.
